In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the 30 kDa protein is a promising candidate for vaccine development against tuberculosis, and that it may be used as an adjunctive therapy to the currently available chemotherapy for tuberculosis.
the 30 kDa antigen is able to restore the T‐cell response and B7‐1/2 costimulatory molecule expression, which are both important for the protective immune response against tuberculosis.
mycobacterial 60/70‐kDa proteins are the major antigens for T‐cell response, but the 30‐kDa secretory protein is a major antigen in the protective immunity of tuberculosis.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the 30 kDa protein, when given as a vaccine, is able to protect mice against virulent challenge of M. tuberculosis, and this protective efficacy is probably mediated via the restoration of T‐cell responses by upregulation of B7‐mediated costimulatory molecules.
the protective efficacy of mycobacterial secretory protein against virulent mycolactone‐containing M. ulcerans is probably due to its ability in enhancing T‐cell responses and B7 costimulation.

the mycobacterial 60 kDa heat shock protein (hsp) and its 30 kDa fragment are capable of restoring the Th1 response and augmenting the costimulatory molecules (B7‐1 and 2), which in turn may contribute to the protection against virulent myco‐bacterial challenge.
The main takeaway from our work is that
30 kDa protein can induce protective immunity against virulent mycolactone‐producing Mycobacterium ulcerans in a murine infection model, and this protection is mediated via Th1‐biased responses.
the 30 kDa protein of mycobacteria is an effective vaccine against tuberculosis and it is able to boost the immune response of mice against tuberculosis.
